question: Soho, London, 1854. An outbreak kills hundreds of people in days. Which disease is it?
answer: Cholera. The famous clue, the Broad Street pump, could not have told you: typhoid travels in dirty water too. What ruled typhoid out was speed. Typhoid takes weeks to kill; cholera can drain a body of water and kill it within a day. John Snow counted 616 dead.
move: Don't ask whether a clue fits. Ask what it rules out.
ask: The last time I was sure, was my best evidence something that fitted every explanation?

clues.text: Over 500 people in a few London streets die within ten days.
No pocks, no swollen glands: violent diarrhoea and vomiting.
Many die within a day of the first cramp.
The dead drank from one pump. The brewery's men drank beer, and lived.

scene.why: Speed decides: typhoid takes weeks to kill, cholera hours. The pump fits typhoid just as well.

source: Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 1855

question: Vienna, 1846. Mothers die of fever far more often in one clinic than in the one next door. What is killing them?
answer: The doctors' hands. Ignaz Semmelweis struck off every rival he could test: the air, the crowding, the priest's bell. What was left was the one difference between the clinics: the doctors came from dissecting corpses, the midwives did not. From May 1847 they washed in chlorine; deaths fell to 13 in 1,000.
move: Strike off the suspects you can test. The one left standing is your lead.
ask: When something goes wrong at home or at work, do I test the rival explanations, or chase the most vivid one?

clues.text: In the doctors' clinic 99 mothers in 1,000 die; next door, with midwives, 39.
Both clinics share one building, one city's air, and take mothers on alternate days.
The midwives' clinic is the more crowded: women beg to be sent there.
The priest stops ringing his bell through the doctors' wards. Deaths don't fall.
A doctor cut by a student's scalpel during an autopsy dies of the same fever.

scene.why: The silent bell struck off the last rival. One difference was left: the doctors came from corpses.

source: Semmelweis, The Etiology of Childbed Fever; Loudon, James Lind Library, 2013
reference: Semmelweis, The Etiology, Concept, and Prophylaxis of Childbed Fever, trans. Carter, University of Wisconsin Press, 1983; https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/articles/ignaz-phillip-semmelweis-studies-of-death-in-childbirth/

question: Yale's Vinland Map shows America half a century before Columbus. When was it really drawn?
answer: Between the 1920s and 1957: it is a forgery. It came bound with a genuine 1440s manuscript, and it shows what Vikings really reached. Neither proves its age. Its ink does: it is laced with anatase, a titanium white first sold as a pigment around 1920. Yale declared it fake in 2021.
move: A real old binding cannot vouch for what is inside it.
ask: What am I trusting because of the company it keeps, rather than its own evidence?

clues.text: It surfaces with a dealer in 1957, bound into a real 1440s manuscript.
It shows Vinland, the coast Vikings reached around 1000, west of Greenland.
Its ink holds anatase, a titanium white first sold as a pigment around 1920.
Yale's 2021 tests find titanium all along the lines, not in a stray speck.

scene.why: The ink decides: no one could use titanium white before about 1920, whatever the binding says.

reference: Yale News, 'Vinland Map is a fake, new analysis confirms', 1 September 2021; https://news.yale.edu/2021/09/01/learning-lessons-fake-vinland-map
